title: Haze from Indonesian fires keeps Singapore’s air unhealthy
hook: Did you know Singapore can take companies to court for smoke from fires in another country?
body: If the sky over Singapore has looked a little yellow lately, you are not imagining it. Smoke from forest and peatland fires in Kalimantan, on the Indonesian side of Borneo, has been drifting across the sea, and the National Environment Agency has repeatedly reported air quality in the unhealthy range. The haze first reached unhealthy levels on 4 September, the first time in nearly three years.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong has said the government is looking into companies that may be responsible for the fires, and could take legal action under the Transboundary Haze Pollution Act where warranted. The law, passed in 2014, is unusual: it lets Singapore hold companies liable for pollution that starts outside its borders, as long as the haze affects Singapore.

Daily life has felt the effects. Seletar Airport recorded 16 flight diversions because of poor visibility, some hawker centres and outdoor restaurants have seen fewer customers, and Marina Bay Sands paused some outdoor attractions and handed out masks. Malaysia, also affected, has offered water bombers, and its Second Finance Minister called the haze “an issue that needs an ASEAN solution”.

Useful words from this story: transboundary (跨境的) means crossing a border; peatland (泥炭地) is wet ground made of dead plants, which can smoulder for weeks once it catches fire; and liable (负有法律责任的) means legally responsible.
